what: The Tirumantiram's eightfold yoga, eight great powers, kāya-citti ('I nourished the body'), 'love is Civam' and 'one family, one God', and the Nandi–Tirumūlar lineage
era: the Siddhar corpus (c. 1400 onward) draws on the Tirumantiram

evidence.detail: Kaṭuveḷi 31 commends the eight-limbed yoga; kāya-citti themes recur (Caṭṭaimuṉi 4; Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 14)
Tirumūlar heads the lists of Siddhars; works are ascribed to him

what: Identification of Maccamuṉi and Kōrakkar with Matsyendranātha and Gorakṣanātha; the goal of the perfected, deathless body; the title 'nātar' for the masters

evidence.detail: the Tamil lists and legends of Maccamuṉi and Kōrakkar
direction and date of contact unsettled

what: Mercurial and mineral alchemy (binding mercury, calcination, transmutation, the alchemical body)

evidence.detail: iracam / rasa, pāṣāṇam, cutti / śodhana, centūram / sindūra

what: The humoral triad, seven body-constituents, six tastes and rejuvenation (rasāyana/kaṟpam)

evidence.detail: the Siddha tradition claims origin from Śiva via Agastya; see dsp:siddha-ayurveda-relation

what: The vital points (varmam), their count and healing uses, ascribed to Agastya

evidence.detail: varmam texts are ascribed to Agastya and taught as a branch of Siddha medicine

what: The critique of caste and ritual, the deathless body, the Light (cōti), and Tāyumāṉavar's camaracam of Vedānta and Siddhānta

evidence.detail: Vallalar venerated Tāyumāṉavar and the Siddhars (low confidence)

what: Worship of the goddess as Bālā (Vālai), Tripurā and Bhuvanā with seed-syllables, and of the Meru of forty-three triangles (Śrīcakra)

evidence.detail: Caṭṭaimuṉi 1–3 names the 43 triangles and the syllables of Vālai, Tripurā, Bhuvanā and Yāmaḷā

what: Vedāntic non-dual language ('I am He', 'pure Vedānta', the Supreme as light and bliss) joined to Śaiva devotion (Tāyumāṉavar's camaracam)
Parallels with the Buddhist siddhas' songs: attack on ritual, caste and scripture; veiled 'twilight' language; the body as the seat of realization

evidence.detail: noted by modern scholars as a parallel; no direct transmission established
